case_title: Nana Keshav Lagad v. State of Maharashtra
accused_socioeconomic_status: Owned and possessed agricultural land adjacent to the complainant's land; no wealth or class finding otherwise stated
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (same village) and land rival; prior enmity and dispute over right of way to adjoining agricultural lands
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; IPC s.324 r/w s.34 (convicted); FIR also cited IPC ss.504, 506, 143, 147, 148, 149 and Bombay Police Act s.37(a) r/w s.135
evidence_type: Eyewitness (two injured/eyewitnesses PW4 and PW5); medical (post-mortem and injury certificates, doctor PW6); recovery of weapons (panch witness PW3); expert/chemical analysis of blood-stained clothing
confession: Admissible portion of the accused's confession was the basis for seizure of cycle chain and stones; the Court did not separately rely on the confession itself
aggravating_circumstances: 19 external and 4 internal injuries to the deceased; group assault with cycle chain and stones; accused reportedly waited on road with intention to assault; injuries to the complainant (11) also noted
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and s.324 r/w s.34; life rigorous imprisonment with Rs.500 fine (default six months) for s.302/34; one year RI with Rs.300 fine (default one month) for s.324/34
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld (judgment dated 16.01.2006 in Criminal Appeal No. 611 of 2003)
offence_finally_established: IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (murder); IPC s.324 r/w s.34 (hurt by dangerous weapon)
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim's family lived in the same village and owned adjoining agricultural land. A dispute existed over the use of a way to reach their fields. On the morning of the incident, the victim and the complainant attempted to reach their field to sow seeds but were obstructed by one of the accused, who abused and threatened them. Later that day, the complainant was told by a neighbour that several of the accused were waiting on a road to assault the victim. The complainant rode a bicycle to the spot and, from about 200 metres away, saw a group beating the victim with a cycle chain and stones while abusing him. The group then turned on the complainant and assaulted him with a cycle chain and stones until a bystander intervened. The complainant found the victim bleeding heavily from the head and with beating marks over the body. The victim was taken to a rural hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem recorded 19 external and 4 internal injuries, all ante-mortem, with death due to shock from haemorrhage. The doctor stated that some injuries were caused by a cycle chain and others by stones, and that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death. The complainant's 11 injuries were certified by the same doctor and attributed to hard blunt objects and a cycle chain. Police arrested the accused, seized blood-stained clothing, and recovered the cycle chain and stones on the basis of information from the accused. Chemical analysis detected human blood on the clothing of the accused and the victim, although the blood group of the accused's sample was inconclusive. A second eyewitness supported the complainant's account. In oral evidence the complainant named fewer assailants than in his written complaint.
physical_harm: Death of the victim (father) from injuries including 19 external and 4 internal injuries; complainant suffered 11 injuries, which were ultimately not serious
number_of_offences: 9 charged (IPC ss.302, 324, 504, 506, 143, 147, 148, 149; Bombay Police Act s.37(a) r/w s.135) per FIR; 2 finally upheld (s.302 r/w 34 and s.324 r/w 34)
premeditation_planning: Court found a coordinated assault with common intention to eliminate the deceased; premeditation not expressly found, though the complaint alleged the accused were waiting on the road to assault the victim
motive: Dispute over right of way to adjoining agricultural lands (enmity); common intention to eliminate the deceased and the complainant
key_evidence_accepted: Complainant PW4's testimony (apart from the two wrongly named assailants); corroborating eyewitness PW5; post-mortem and injury evidence of doctor PW6 linking injuries to cycle chain and stones; expert blood report on clothing; panch witness PW3 on recovery
witness_credibility: PW4 found credible despite wrongly naming two accused, which was admitted fairly; PW5 found to merit acceptance on par with PW4; PW3 panch witness's version found truthfully and fully corroborated despite being alleged a stock witness
trial_duration: offence: 04.10.2002; trial judgment: 21.08.2003; High Court: 16.01.2006; Supreme Court: 03.07.2013
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Karanjkar, M.Y. Deshmukh, Nikilesh Kumar, Shrikand R. Deshmukh, Rameshwar Prasad Goyal. State: Shankar Chillarge, Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR (CR No.249 of 2002) registered; inquest and arrests made; charge-sheet filed and case committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court (Sessions Court, Sessions Case No.191 of 2002): convicted and sentenced; High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence upheld; Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Case falls under Section 300 thirdly, established by the doctor's evidence that the injuries caused death; PW5's corroboration, medical evidence and proof of weapons support the conviction
defence_argument: Sole eyewitness PW4 unreliable due to discrepancies (two names omitted); injuries and weapons do not correlate; panch witness PW3 not established; blood finding on shirt not proved by expert evidence; s.34 not attracted
legal_principle_applied: Conviction need not rest solely on uncorroborated injured eyewitness; partial inaccuracy does not warrant rejecting whole testimony where corroborated by medical and other evidence; accused must explain bloodstains on clothing (s.313); s.34 applicable where common intention shown
precedent_relied_upon: Vadivelu Thevar v. State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614 (distinguished, held inapplicable); Abdul Sayeed v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2010) 10 SCC 259 (held inapplicable)
judicial_aggravating_factors: Coordinated vengeance and multiple injuries inflicted to ensure the deceased did not survive
